screens.title: Introduction to Indexes and B-Trees
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn what an index does, how MongoDB builds and uses B-tree indexes, and why indexes are a foundational performance tool. Imagine a large library without a catalog: searching shelf by shelf would take ages. An index gives MongoDB a sorted map to the documents you need so queries can avoid scanning every record. We'll also practice creating a single-field index, examine real query plans with the explain method, and discuss common trade-offs such as increased write overhead and disk usage. I'll show a concrete example: indexing a products collection to turn a slow collection scan into a fast index scan. You will also learn practical safety steps like using the background option for large collections and verifying index usage with execution statistics. By the end of this chapter you'll recognize when an index will help, how MongoDB stores index keys in a B-tree, and how to read the basic indicators in an explain output. Think about a query you run frequently: could an index reduce its latency?

screens.title: Why Indexes Matter
screens.narratorSegment: An index is a data structure that stores a small, ordered subset of a collection's data so MongoDB can find documents much faster than by scanning every record. Conceptually, an index maps field values to pointers that identify documents. This is critical in read-heavy applications where response time matters. For example, searching millions of users by email without an index forces MongoDB to perform a full collection scan, checking each document until it finds a match. With an index on the email field, MongoDB uses the sorted keys to jump directly to matching documents. A common misconception is that adding more indexes is always beneficial. In reality each index consumes disk space and requires updates when documents change, which increases write cost. So indexing is a strategic trade-off: add indexes where queries benefit most. Concrete example: if your application frequently looks up users by email or customer_id, a single-field index on that field will usually produce dramatic read improvements. Takeaway: think of indexes as selective accelerators that you apply where they produce measurable gains; always validate with explain before assuming a speedup.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Why Indexes Matter
Definition

An index stores sorted keys and pointers so MongoDB can find documents without scanning the whole collection. It is the primary mechanism to reduce read latency.

Key bullets
  • Indexes map field values to document pointers for fast lookups.
  • They reduce disk I/O by keeping tree height low and traversable in few steps.
  • Every write to an indexed field must update the index, adding overhead.
  • Apply indexes where frequent queries will benefit measurably.
Example
Lookup users by email will be slow without an index; indexing email turns that lookup into a direct traversal of the index.
Common mistake
Over-indexing increases write latency and disk use without matching read gains.
Key Takeaway

Index where queries are frequent and measurable, then verify with explain to prove benefit.

Analogy & Visuals
Library without catalog
Full scan: check every shelf, slow for large collections.
Library with catalog
Index: go to the shelf directly, fast lookup.
Why it matters: user-facing queries, analytics, and API endpoints often rely on fast lookups. Indexes are the primary lever to reduce latency for those operations.

screens.title: B-tree Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: A B-tree is the default structure MongoDB uses for most indexes because it stays balanced and shallow while storing many keys. The core idea: each node contains multiple keys and pointers to child nodes, which reduces the height of the tree compared with a binary tree. Searches proceed top-down: the engine compares the search key to the node's keys, picks the child pointer that leads closer to the match, and repeats until a leaf node is reached. Leaf nodes contain key-to-document pointer mappings. This multi-way branching lowers disk input and output because fewer nodes need to be read to find a key. A concrete image: imagine a phonebook organized by blocks of letters; you pick the block, then the page, then the name. A common misconception is thinking B-tree nodes hold whole documents — they do not. B-tree nodes hold keys and pointers only, keeping the index compact. In practice, that compactness and the shallow height are what let MongoDB perform index scans in logarithmic time even for large collections. Ask yourself: for a heavily queried field, could a B-tree index turn many expensive reads into a few predictable lookups?

keyIdea.title: Balanced, shallow tree
keyIdea.text: B-trees store keys and pointers in multi-key nodes so traversal requires few node reads even for large datasets.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › B-tree Fundamentals
Process: searching a B-tree
  1. Compare the search key to the keys in the root node to pick the correct child pointer.
  2. Follow the child pointer and compare against that node's keys, repeating until a leaf node.
  3. At the leaf, use the key-to-document pointer mapping to fetch matching documents.
Because each node stores multiple keys, the number of levels is small. Fewer levels means fewer disk reads and faster lookups even on large collections.
Concrete example
If a node holds 100 keys, one root lookup narrows you to one of many child ranges; you rarely descend more than three or four levels for very large sets.
Visual breakdown
Root & internal nodes
Contain sorted keys and pointers to children; guide traversal.
Leaf nodes
Contain keys mapped to document pointers; used to fetch results.
Key Takeaway

B-tree nodes pack many keys so searches touch few nodes. That compactness is the reason indexes scale.

screens.title: Nodes, Keys, and Leaves
screens.narratorSegment: An index's leaves are where the key-to-document mappings live. Internal nodes hold key ranges and pointers to children, and the tree is balanced so all leaves sit at the same depth. When you create a single-field index, MongoDB extracts that field's values and inserts them into the B-tree as keys. Those keys in the leaves reference the physical location of documents, either by record id or storage pointer depending on internal storage details. This separation keeps the index small compared to full documents, which is why index scans can be much faster than collection scans. A useful concrete check: use getIndexes to confirm an index exists; then run explain in executionStats mode to see if the winningPlan shows IXSCAN, which means the engine traversed the index rather than scanning every document. Misconception to avoid: indexes do not replace the need for correct query predicates. An index only helps if your query matches the indexed keys in an indexable way—certain patterns like leading wildcards in regular expressions can prevent index use. Final thought: leaves are the direct link from keys to documents—optimizing the size and selectivity of keys at that level gives you the most benefit.

Hierarchy: index structure
Root
Starting point of searches, contains top keys.
Internal nodes
Guide traversal with key ranges and child pointers.
Leaf nodes
Contain key-to-document pointer mappings used to fetch results.
Verification steps: run db.collection.getIndexes() to list indexes and run a target query with explain('executionStats') to confirm IXSCAN in winningPlan. If you see COLLSCAN, the query did not use an index.
Example check
After creating an index on category, re-run your category query with explain and compare executionTimeMillis to prove impact.
Pitfall
A query that doesn't reference the exact indexed field or uses a non-indexable predicate may still force a collection scan.
Quick checklist
  • Confirm index exists with getIndexes()
  • Use explain('executionStats') to inspect winningPlan.stage
  • Look for IXSCAN to verify index usage

screens.title: Creating a Single-Field Index
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a single-field index in the MongoDB shell uses a clear command pattern: specify the collection, the field, and the sort order. For example, to index an email field in ascending order you use the createIndex call with the field mapped to 1 for ascending. In production, building an index on a large collection can be resource intensive. To avoid blocking ongoing operations, you can build the index in the background. This runs the build without preventing other reads and writes, though it may take longer to complete. A practical verification step after building is to run getIndexes to see the new index metadata. A common misconception is that createIndex is instantaneous: on large collections it can take time and consume C P U and input and output. Also understand that adding an index will increase the cost of writes that affect that indexed field because the index must be updated as documents change. In the code walkthrough area you'll find the exact shell commands used in the hands-on activity. Use these as a template and adapt to your field names and production safety needs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Creating a Single-Field Index
Command pattern
db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 })

// For production builds on large collections
// db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { background: true })

// Verify indexes
// db.users.getIndexes()
Notes: use 1 for ascending and -1 for descending. The background option prevents blocking other operations during the build, though it may take longer. After creation, verify with getIndexes before relying on the index in production queries.
Practical tips
  • Prefer indexes on fields used frequently in equality or range predicates.
  • Avoid indexing low-selectivity fields that return many documents.
  • Remember that writes to indexed fields update the index.
Why it matters

Proper index creation and verification is the first step to measurable query improvement.

screens.title: Using explain() to Inspect Query Plans
screens.narratorSegment: The explain method is the evidence you need to understand a query's performance. When you append explain with executionStats to a find operation, MongoDB runs the query and returns the plan it used and actual execution metrics. Look for winningPlan. stage: IXSCAN to confirm index usage; if you see winningPlan. stage: COLLSCAN it means the query scanned every document. ExecutionStats includes executionTimeMillis and totalDocsExamined, which let you compare before-and-after results. For a concrete workflow: run the query without an index and record executionTimeMillis and the stage; create the appropriate index; then rerun the same query and compare. A common misconception is reading explain's queryPlanner-only mode and assuming it reflects actual runtime; executionStats shows what actually happened and is the better choice to measure effect. Also be mindful of query predicates and data types—if a field's type does not match the query value type, the optimizer may not use the index. Use explain('executionStats') as the final arbiter when deciding whether an index provided real-world improvement. Using explain() to Inspect Query Plans means use explain('executionstats') to see winningplan.stage, executiontimemillis, and documents scanned to confirm index impact.. In practical terms, executionstats shows whether a query used ixscan or collscan and how long it took. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Using explain()
Example explain command
db.products.find({ category: "Category 50" }).explain("executionStats")

// Inspect the output for:
// winningPlan.stage  => "IXSCAN" or "COLLSCAN"
// executionStats.executionTimeMillis
// executionStats.totalDocsExamined
Use executionStats to measure real execution. QueryPlanner mode can show possible plans, but executionStats reports what actually happened during the run.
Interpretation guide
  • IXSCAN in winningPlan.stage indicates the index was used.
  • COLLSCAN indicates a full collection scan and likely poor performance.
  • Compare executionTimeMillis before and after adding an index to measure benefit.
Quick tip

If explain shows COLLSCAN after you added an index, verify the index exists and that your query predicate matches the indexed field and types.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Insert Sample Data
Starter insertion script
use cohortia_shop;
db.products.drop(); // Clear previous data if any

let products = [];
for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
  products.push({
    name: `Product ${i}`,
    category: `Category ${i % 100}`,
    price: Math.floor(Math.random() * 1000) + 1,
    sku: `SKU-${Math.floor(Math.random() * 1000000)}`,
    description: `Description for product ${i}`,
    createdAt: new Date()
  });
}
db.products.insertMany(products);
print("Inserted 100,000 products.");
Run this in a development environment. The script builds a varied set of categories so you can test range and equality queries on category values. Use this dataset to capture explain outputs before and after indexing.
Measurement steps
  1. Insert sample data to create a realistic baseline.
  2. Run the target query and save explain('executionStats') output.
  3. Create the index on the queried field and re-run explain for comparison.

Empirical measurement is the only reliable way to prove an index improves your specific query patterns.

screens.title: Query Before and After Index
screens.narratorSegment: A direct comparison shows the value of an index. First, run the query on the unindexed field and capture explain executionStats: you will typically see winningPlan. stage equal to COLLSCAN, a high executionTimeMillis, and a large totalDocsExamined. That is your baseline. Next, create an index on the field used in the predicate and rerun the same explain. You should now see winningPlan. stage equal to IXSCAN, a much lower executionTimeMillis, and far fewer documents examined. These numbers are the evidence you need to justify the index. A key misconception is assuming the index will always speed every query; the optimizer chooses plans based on estimated cost and selectivity. If the predicate is poorly selective or if the index does not support the query shape, you may not see the expected IXSCAN. Always compare the exact query and explain output before and after. Concrete example: querying Category 50 on the products collection should transition from COLLSCAN to IXSCAN after creating an index on category and show a large reduction in executionTimeMillis. Query Before and After Index means use executiontimemillis and totaldocsexamined from explain to quantify index benefit when winningplan.stage changes to ixscan.. In practical terms, compare explain outputs to see collscan vs ixscan and the performance change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Index Costs and Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Indexes are not free. While they provide direct read benefits by enabling IXSCAN, they also consume disk space and add overhead to write operations because inserts, updates, and deletes must maintain the index structure. When you add an index on a high-write field, each write operation requires updating the B-tree, which increases latency and C P U use. Another trade-off is storage: the index stores a compact but additional representation of field values and pointers. A common mistake is creating indexes on low-selectivity fields—those that return many documents for a given key—because the read benefit will be small while the write cost remains. To decide whether to add an index, consider query frequency, selectivity, and operational cost. A practical approach: measure read latency improvements with explain and weigh them against increased write time and storage growth. In production, monitor write latency and disk usage after creating an index and be ready to roll back if the trade-off is unfavorable. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Index Costs and Trade-offs
Trade-off breakdown
  • Read benefit: faster lookups via IXSCAN when the query matches the index.
  • Write overhead: index updates on insert/update/delete for indexed fields.
  • Storage: indexes consume disk space to store keys and pointers.
  • Selectivity matters: high-selectivity fields yield the largest read gains.
Example decision
If a field is queried hundreds of times per second and returns few documents per query, an index is likely worth the write cost. If a field returns many records, reconsider.
Monitoring after index creation
Track write latency, CPU, and disk usage after adding an index. Compare metrics to the baseline to ensure the trade-off is acceptable.
Quick tip

Run targeted explain tests and small production trials before adding indexes to critical collections.

screens.title: When Indexes Are Not Used
screens.narratorSegment: Indexes only help when queries are written in an indexable way. Common scenarios that prevent index use include queries that use regular expressions with leading wildcards, such as patterns that start with an arbitrary prefix. Those patterns cannot be satisfied efficiently by a B-tree because the search key is not anchored. Another frequent cause is type mismatches: if the indexed field contains date objects but your query uses a string, the optimizer may not match the index. Typos in field names used in createIndex versus the query are an easy but critical mistake—if the field names don't match, the index is invisible to the query planner. When you see explain showing COLLSCAN, follow a checklist: verify the index exists with getIndexes, confirm field names and data types match, and ensure the query shape is supported by the index. If those checks pass but performance is still poor, consider compound indexes or adjusting the query pattern. The bottom line is: build the right index and write queries that let MongoDB use it. When Indexes Are Not Used means avoid leading wildcard regex, check types and field names, and verify index existence to ensure the optimizer can use an index.. In practical terms, regex patterns, type mismatches, and incorrect field names can prevent index use. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › When Indexes Are Not Used
Common causes of COLLSCAN
  • Regex with a leading wildcard that cannot be anchored to the index.
  • Field name typos between the index definition and the query.
  • Data type mismatches between stored values and query values.
  • Query shapes that do not align with indexed prefixes or compound index order.
Checklist
If you see COLLSCAN, run getIndexes(), check field names and types, and rewrite the query to match the indexed fields where possible.
Example pitfall
Index on email will not help a query using a pattern that searches for an email domain with a leading wildcard; instead, index-supported queries should start with anchored values.
Warning

Never assume an index will be used; always confirm with explain('executionStats').

screens.title: Production Considerations: background builds and verification

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Production Considerations
Safe build sequence
  1. Plan the index and estimate the build cost on a staging dataset.
  2. Create the index with background:true on large collections to avoid blocking.
  3. Run db.collection.getIndexes() to verify the index exists and inspect its options.
  4. Rerun explain('executionStats') for target queries and monitor metrics.
If performance degrades after adding an index, consider dropping the index or adjusting it and re-measuring. Always roll back with a recovery plan.
Commands for production
// Create index safely
// db.collection.createIndex({ field: 1 }, { background: true })

// Verify
// db.collection.getIndexes()

// Remove index if needed
// db.collection.dropIndex({ field: 1 })
Why it matters

Safe builds and verification reduce the risk of adding indexes to live systems and provide measurable evidence of benefit.

Keep these ideas together when planning indexing work so you create measurable, safe improvements to query performance.

In this lesson you'll learn what an index does, how MongoDB builds and uses B-tree indexes, and why indexes are a foundational performance tool. Imagine a large library without a catalog: searching shelf by shelf would take ages. An index gives MongoDB a sorted map to the documents you need so queries can avoid scanning every record. We'll also practice creating a single-field index, examine real query plans with the explain method, and discuss common trade-offs such as increased write overhead and disk usage. I'll show a concrete example: indexing a products collection to turn a slow collection scan into a fast index scan. You will also learn practical safety steps like using the background option for large collections and verifying index usage with execution statistics. By the end of this chapter you'll recognize when an index will help, how MongoDB stores index keys in a B-tree, and how to read the basic indicators in an explain output. Think about a query you run frequently: could an index reduce its latency?

These objectives guide the practice you will do in this chapter. First, you'll explain the core purpose and benefits of indexes in MongoDB: how they replace costly full collection scans with direct lookups and why read-heavy workloads benefit most. Second, you'll describe the B-tree data structure: its multi-level nodes, sorted keys, and why its shallow height reduces disk input and output. Third, you'll create and verify single-field indexes on a collection using the createIndex command and confirm the index exists. Fourth, you'll use the explain method with execution statistics to analyze query plans and identify whether a query used an index or fell back to a collection scan. Each objective includes a simple example or verification step so you can show evidence of learning, and each skill matters because indexing decisions directly affect read latency, write overhead, and disk usage in production systems.

These objectives focus on evidence and safe practices. You will learn to use the explain method to read a query's winning plan and execution statistics. That includes identifying the winningPlan. stage field, where IXSCAN means an index was used and COLLSCAN means a full collection scan occurred. You will practice creating an index safely on large collections using the background option so the build doesn't block operations, and you will verify index presence with getIndexes. Finally, you'll practice reasoning about trade-offs: every index speeds certain reads but raises write cost and disk usage. The chapter provides a hands-on activity inserting many documents into a products collection to make the performance difference visible with explain outputs before and after an index. These skills are practical: on an active system you must prove an index improves the actual queries you care about and be mindful of the cost to writes and storage.

An index is a data structure that stores a small, ordered subset of a collection's data so MongoDB can find documents much faster than by scanning every record. Conceptually, an index maps field values to pointers that identify documents. This is critical in read-heavy applications where response time matters. For example, searching millions of users by email without an index forces MongoDB to perform a full collection scan, checking each document until it finds a match. With an index on the email field, MongoDB uses the sorted keys to jump directly to matching documents. A common misconception is that adding more indexes is always beneficial. In reality each index consumes disk space and requires updates when documents change, which increases write cost. So indexing is a strategic trade-off: add indexes where queries benefit most. Concrete example: if your application frequently looks up users by email or customer_id, a single-field index on that field will usually produce dramatic read improvements. Takeaway: think of indexes as selective accelerators that you apply where they produce measurable gains; always validate with explain before assuming a speedup.

A B-tree is the default structure MongoDB uses for most indexes because it stays balanced and shallow while storing many keys. The core idea: each node contains multiple keys and pointers to child nodes, which reduces the height of the tree compared with a binary tree. Searches proceed top-down: the engine compares the search key to the node's keys, picks the child pointer that leads closer to the match, and repeats until a leaf node is reached. Leaf nodes contain key-to-document pointer mappings. This multi-way branching lowers disk input and output because fewer nodes need to be read to find a key. A concrete image: imagine a phonebook organized by blocks of letters; you pick the block, then the page, then the name. A common misconception is thinking B-tree nodes hold whole documents — they do not. B-tree nodes hold keys and pointers only, keeping the index compact. In practice, that compactness and the shallow height are what let MongoDB perform index scans in logarithmic time even for large collections. Ask yourself: for a heavily queried field, could a B-tree index turn many expensive reads into a few predictable lookups?

An index's leaves are where the key-to-document mappings live. Internal nodes hold key ranges and pointers to children, and the tree is balanced so all leaves sit at the same depth. When you create a single-field index, MongoDB extracts that field's values and inserts them into the B-tree as keys. Those keys in the leaves reference the physical location of documents, either by record id or storage pointer depending on internal storage details. This separation keeps the index small compared to full documents, which is why index scans can be much faster than collection scans. A useful concrete check: use getIndexes to confirm an index exists; then run explain in executionStats mode to see if the winningPlan shows IXSCAN, which means the engine traversed the index rather than scanning every document. Misconception to avoid: indexes do not replace the need for correct query predicates. An index only helps if your query matches the indexed keys in an indexable way—certain patterns like leading wildcards in regular expressions can prevent index use. Final thought: leaves are the direct link from keys to documents—optimizing the size and selectivity of keys at that level gives you the most benefit.

For example, to index an email field in ascending order you use the createIndex call with the field mapped to 1 for ascending. In production, building an index on a large collection can be resource intensive. To avoid blocking ongoing operations, you can build the index in the background. This runs the build without preventing other reads and writes, though it may take longer to complete. A practical verification step after building is to run getIndexes to see the new index metadata. A common misconception is that createIndex is instantaneous: on large collections it can take time and consume C P U and input and output. Also understand that adding an index will increase the cost of writes that affect that indexed field because the index must be updated as documents change. In the code walkthrough area you'll find the exact shell commands used in the hands-on activity. Use these as a template and adapt to your field names and production safety needs.

Here are the core concepts to keep in mind. First, an index is a special data structure that stores a compact, ordered subset of collection data to speed queries. Second, MongoDB uses a B-tree for most indexes, which remains shallow because nodes contain many keys; this reduces disk input and output for lookups. Third, use createIndex to build single-field indexes and consider background:true for safety on large collections. Fourth, use explain with executionStats to determine whether a query used IXSCAN or fell back to COLLSCAN and to measure executionTimeMillis and documents examined. Fifth, indexes come with trade-offs: they increase write overhead and disk usage, so index selectively where queries benefit most. Finally, common pitfalls include type mismatches, typos, and non-indexable query shapes such as leading-wildcard regex.
